title: Tell me a story: why great storytelling beats being right, and what it means for marketing
summary: Jason Cohen uses Malcolm Gladwell's success despite debunked theories to argue that stories persuade more than correct logic does. His takeaway is Seth Godin's: marketing is telling a good story, and most other factors are second-order effects.

principles.text: Marketing is telling a good story; most other factors are second-order effects.
principles.quote: So it's just another way to reinforce Seth's admonishment that marketing should be defined as telling a good story. Sometimes everything else is a second-order effect.

principles.text: Great stories carry audiences past weak or wrong conclusions; people accept the argument after being captivated.
principles.quote: After being beguiled with interesting, provocative stories, the reader is happy to receive Gladwell's unproven, non-sequitur conclusions.

principles.text: Story quality can make content worth consuming even when its logic is flawed.
principles.quote: The stories are so good, they're worth reading anyway.

principles.text: Correlation is not causation; check whether a result happened everywhere regardless of your intervention before crediting your tactic.
principles.quote: correlations don't imply causal relationships. Just because you did X and Y happened afterward doesn't mean X necessarily caused Y.

principles.text: Defending a flawed theory with 'we only see a piece of the picture' is a cop-out; admit error instead.
principles.quote: To me this is a cop-out, too embarrassing to just say, "Yeah, it's wrong, but at least it had a lot of great stories."
